title: Multiplication by a central torus with semisimple quotient and the derived group
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme], and let $R\subset G$ be a central torus, meaning a central closed subgroup isomorphic over $F$ to $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$. Assume the fppf sheaf quotient $G/R$ is represented by a semisimple $F$-group scheme; this quotient is the sheafification of $A\mapsto G(A)/R(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. Let $D=G^{\mathrm{der}}$ denote the smallest closed subgroup scheme through which the commutator morphism $(x,y)\mapsto xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ factors. Then $D$ is smooth, connected, affine, of finite type and semisimple, and the multiplication homomorphism $m:R\times_F D\to G$, $(t,d)\mapsto td$, is faithfully flat with finite central kernel of multiplicative type. Its kernel is isomorphic to the scheme-theoretic intersection $R\cap D$ by $a\mapsto(a,a^{-1})$. Here a semisimple group is a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup scheme; solvable means that its successive derived subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. A multiplicative isogeny means a homomorphism whose pullback on coordinate algebras is faithfully flat and whose scheme-theoretic kernel is finite and of multiplicative type. Faithfully flat means that extension of scalars is exact and detects zero modules. Finite means having finite-dimensional coordinate algebra. A finite group scheme is of multiplicative type if, after extension to an algebraic closure, it is diagonalizable: it is isomorphic to $D(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ for a finite abelian group $M$, with comultiplication $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$ on the group-algebra basis. Central means commuting with every group element after every scalar extension.

source.place: Proposition 12.46(a),(b), printed pp.245--246; Theorem 21.50 (semisimple groups are perfect); Proposition 19.21(b),(c), printed pp.401--402; proof of Proposition 21.60(a)--(c), printed p.442; Sections 12.9--12.10 and 12.14 on subgroups of split tori. The kernel of multiplication is the inverse diagonal of the scheme-theoretic intersection.

proof.text: Write $Q=G/R$; since $R$ is central it is normal in $G$. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] for $R\subseteq G$, the fppf quotient $G/R$ is represented by an affine group scheme of finite type whose quotient homomorphism is faithfully flat with scheme-theoretic kernel $R$; as $Q$ represents the same sheaf compatibly with the projections, $q:G\to Q$ is faithfully flat with $\ker q=R$. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup] to $G$ and $Q$: their derived subgroups are smooth connected closed affine groups of finite type, and their $F$-points are the abstract commutator subgroups. Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-group-perfect] to $Q$; it gives $Q^{\mathrm{der}}=Q$. Since $Q$ is smooth and $q$ is faithfully flat, [lem-sfb-affine-group-homomorphism-image] makes $q$ surjective on $F$-points. Given an expression of an element of $Q(F)$ as a product of commutators, lift the entries of those commutators to $G(F)$; their commutator product belongs to $D(F)$ and maps to that element. Thus $q|_D:D(F)\to Q(F)$ is surjective. The same rational-point criterion, with smooth target $Q$, makes $q|_D:D\to Q$ faithfully flat.

source.place: Proposition 12.46(b), printed pp.245--246; Corollary 21.50, printed p.440; Propositions 5.47 and 6.20(b); quotient projection by the existing node lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-central-torus-faithful-weight-blocks] for $(G,R)$, obtaining $\rho$ and $V=\bigoplus_i V_i$ with characters $\chi_i$ and positive integers $n_i=\dim_F V_i$. The determinant of each block action is a homomorphism $\delta_i:G\to\mathbf G_m$. Since its target is commutative, [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup] says that $\delta_i|_D=1$ as a morphism of group schemes. For the scheme-theoretic intersection $K=R\cap D$ this gives $\chi_i|_K^{n_i}=1$ over every $F$-algebra, rather than merely on geometric points.

The closed immersion $(\chi_i):R\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_m^s$ restricts to a closed immersion of $K$ and factors through $\prod_i\mu_{n_i}$ by the preceding equations. In coordinates this gives a surjection $F[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_s^{\pm1}]/(z_i^{n_i}-1)_i\twoheadrightarrow F[K]$: the map before imposing the relations is surjective, so it stays surjective after imposing relations that vanish on $K$. The source is spanned over $F$ by the finitely many monomials $\prod_i z_i^{a_i}$ with $0\leq a_i<n_i$ (replace inverses using $z_i^{-1}=z_i^{n_i-1}$). Thus $F[K]$ is finite-dimensional. This proves scheme-theoretic finiteness even when the characteristic divides some $n_i$.

source.place: Proposition 12.46(a), proof, printed p.246 (coordinate refinement of the scalar-matrix argument)

proof.text: The kernel of $q|_D$ is $D\times_G\ker q=D\times_G R=K$, since $\ker q=R$ by step 1 ([lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]). Step 1 makes $q|_D$ faithfully flat, and step 3 makes its kernel finite. Both $D$ and $Q$ are smooth connected affine groups of finite type, as required by [lem-sfb-semisimple-isogeny-source]. Applying that lemma to $D\to Q$ proves that $D$ is semisimple.

source.place: Lemma 19.14, printed p.400; proof of Proposition 21.60(b) implies (c), printed p.442

proof.text: Centrality of $R$ makes multiplication $m:R\times_F D\to G$ a group-scheme homomorphism: $(t_1d_1)(t_2d_2)=(t_1t_2)(d_1d_2)$ over every scalar algebra. For $g\in G(F)$ choose $d\in D(F)$ with $q(d)=q(g)$ by step 1. Then $t=gd^{-1}\in\ker(q)(F)=R(F)$ and $g=td$. Hence $m$ is surjective on $F$-points. Its target $G$ is smooth, so [lem-sfb-affine-group-homomorphism-image] makes $m$ faithfully flat.

For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$, a pair $(t,d)\in R(A)\times D(A)$ is in $\ker(m)(A)$ exactly when $d=t^{-1}$. It then determines $t\in K(A)$, and conversely $a\in K(A)$ gives $(a,a^{-1})$. These formulas commute with every algebra map and use the subgroup inclusions and inversion morphisms, so define inverse morphisms $K\simeq\ker(m)$. Both $a$ and $a^{-1}$ are central in $G$; therefore $(a,a^{-1})$ commutes with every $(t,d)$ after every scalar extension. This proves centrality of the scheme-theoretic kernel, including infinitesimal elements.

source.place: Proposition 12.46(b), sequence (78) and its kernel identification

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] to the closed subgroup $K\subset R\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. It gives $K\simeq D(M)$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$, which is finite because $F[K]$ is finite-dimensional by step 3. Step 6 identifies this finite diagonalizable group with $\ker(m)$. This is precisely the claimed finite central kernel of multiplicative type.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(c), printed pp.233--234; Proposition 12.46, printed pp.245--246
